promptText: What is prompt injection, in the chapter's precise framing?
options: A technique for making a model respond faster by shortening its prompt

Text supplied to a model — whether typed by a user or embedded in retrieved/tool content — that contains instruction-like language causing the model to deviate from intended behavior, because the model has no reliable built-in way to distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted data in its context
A method for injecting additional training data into a model after deployment
A vulnerability that only affects models fine-tuned on proprietary datasets
explanation: The model's context window has no built-in mechanism that preserves trust levels once text is inside it — role labels are a soft, trained signal, not a hard guarantee.

promptText: Why can't prompt injection be fixed the same way parameterized queries fixed SQL injection?
options: Because SQL injection was never actually solved by parameterized queries

Because a database driver enforces a protocol-level, mechanical separation between query structure and data values, while an LLM's prompt is one undifferentiated stream of tokens with no equivalent hard boundary — role labels are a trained, soft signal, not an unbreakable guarantee
Because parameterized queries require a GPU, which LLMs don't have access to
Because prompt injection only affects models trained before 2022
explanation: This is the chapter's central historical irony: LLMs reopen the exact vulnerability class the industry spent twenty years eliminating from SQL, but there is no equivalent of a prepared statement for natural-language prompts.

promptText: What is the difference between direct and indirect prompt injection?
options: Direct injection only affects chatbots; indirect injection only affects agents with tools

In direct injection the attacker is the user typing adversarial text directly; in indirect injection the attacker plants malicious instructions inside content a legitimate user's system will later retrieve or fetch, so the victim never sees the attack themselves
Direct injection requires SQL access; indirect injection requires only HTML access
There is no meaningful difference — both terms describe the same attack
explanation: Indirect injection is considered the more dangerous, less intuitive case precisely because the victim did nothing wrong — the attack arrives through data the system was designed to trust enough to read.

promptText: What does "excessive agency" mean in the OWASP LLM taxonomy, and what is its primary mitigation?
options: It means the model refuses too many legitimate requests; mitigated by loosening safety filters

It means an agent has been granted more autonomy, tool access, or unsupervised action scope than its actual task requires; mitigated by the principle of least privilege — narrow tool scoping, bounds-checked arguments, and human approval for high-risk actions
It means the model generates responses that are too long; mitigated by output length limits
It only applies to multi-agent systems, never to a single agent
explanation: The target security property is not 'the model is well-behaved' (unguaranteeable) but 'even if the model is fully compromised, the blast radius is bounded by what its granted tools and credentials can actually do.'

promptText: Why should an LLM agent never see a raw API key or credential inside its own context, even one it technically "needs" to call a tool?
options: Because credentials placed in context automatically expire after one turn

Because anything in the model's context can, through a bug, a successful injection, or an unexpected completion, end up in the model's output, so putting a real credential there turns every such failure mode into a credential leak — the tool-execution layer should hold and inject credentials, never the model
Because credentials are always too long to fit in a context window
Because MCP explicitly forbids credentials from being valid JSON
explanation: The model should only ever see and produce the logical parameters of a tool call (which account, which record), never the secret used to authenticate that call — the orchestration layer attaches real credentials outside the model's view.

promptText: What is "unbounded consumption" (sometimes called denial-of-wallet) as an LLM-specific risk?
options: A model that refuses to answer any question involving numbers

An attack or accidental misuse pattern where a service is driven to consume far more compute/tokens than intended, showing up as an inflated bill rather than a classic outage, since most LLM APIs bill per token
A vulnerability found only in on-premises, self-hosted models
A technique for compressing prompts to reduce token usage
explanation: This is the LLM-era analogue of denial of service — a single crafted request (e.g., one inducing very long reasoning chains) can cost a large multiple of an average request without necessarily looking abnormal at the request-count level.

promptText: Why does stacking three separate LLM-based content filters not automatically give you three independent layers of defense-in-depth?
options: Because LLM-based filters are always 100% accurate individually, so stacking them adds no value at all

Because if all three filters are themselves LLM-based classifiers reasoning about 'does this look like an attack,' they share the same underlying failure mechanism — a payload sophisticated enough to fool one is disproportionately likely to fool the others too, since they are correlated, not independent
Because MCP technically limits a system to at most two active filters
Because content filters can only be applied to output, never to input
explanation: The mathematical benefit of defense-in-depth (multiplying miss rates) only holds when layers fail independently — genuine layered defense requires at least one layer that is not model-based at all, such as a deterministic tool-execution allow-list.

promptText: In the defense-in-depth chain against indirect prompt injection, which link is described as the strongest because it does not depend on the model behaving correctly?
options: An input classifier that flags likely injection attempts before the prompt reaches the model
Delimiter-based framing that labels retrieved content as untrusted reference data

The tool-execution layer and identity/authorization layer — e.g., enforcing that a sendEmail tool can only send to allow-listed addresses, and executing every call under the authenticated user's real permissions
Using a more capable foundation model with stronger instruction-following
explanation: Every defense upstream of the model call is a probabilistic reduction in attack likelihood; only tool-layer allow-listing and identity-scoped authorization are deterministic, code-enforced guarantees that hold even if the model is fully compromised.

promptText: What is the "confused deputy" problem as it applies to an LLM agent holding broad tool credentials?
options: A bug where the agent literally becomes confused and stops responding to any input

A program with more privilege than the party instructing it gets tricked into misusing that privilege on the instructing party's behalf; an LLM agent is a textbook confused deputy since it often holds broad service credentials but takes 'instructions' from untrusted sources like injected content
A protocol version mismatch between an MCP client and server
A situation where two agents disagree about which one should execute a tool call
explanation: An attacker who can't directly access a protected resource can get the agent to access it instead, laundering their unauthorized request through the agent's legitimate-looking privilege — this concept predates LLMs by decades.

promptText: An agent has both a search_customer_db tool and a send_slack_message tool, neither dangerous in isolation. Why do they become a real exfiltration risk when combined, and what is the recommended defense?
options: They are not actually risky together since each individually passed review; no special defense is needed

Under an injected instruction they compose into 'read sensitive data, then transmit it to an attacker-controlled channel' — the defense is treating tool combinations, not just individual tools, as the unit of risk analysis, e.g. requiring send-type tool destinations to be validated against a model-uncontrollable allow-list
The only fix is removing all send-capable tools from every agent permanently
This risk is fully eliminated simply by adding a stronger system prompt
explanation: This is 'tool composition risk' — reviewing tools individually and reviewing the graph of what data can flow between them are different exercises, and most reviews only do the former.

promptText: Why is a database_query tool that accepts raw SQL considered an excessive-agency design flaw, independent of whether prompt injection ever succeeds against it?
options: Raw SQL tools are always slower than parameterized function calls

The tool's own surface area is already too broad for the stated task — arbitrary SQL execution grants read/write/delete access across every table, when the agent's actual job is likely a small set of specific lookups; the fix is narrow, purpose-built functions rather than better injection defenses alone
SQL cannot be represented in a JSON Schema, so the tool is technically invalid
Raw SQL tools cannot be logged for audit purposes
explanation: Even setting aside whether the model can be manipulated into emitting a malicious query, the tool's API surface is itself the attack surface — designing narrow, parameterized tools removes the raw-SQL blast radius regardless of injection defenses.

promptText: Why is egress filtering (an allow-list of outbound network destinations) often a more effective control against data exfiltration than trying to detect exfiltration intent in the prompt?
options: Because egress filtering is cheaper to implement than any prompt-based defense

Because detecting intent in the prompt is a probabilistic, adversarial game the attacker can iterate against indefinitely, whereas a deterministic allow-list of outbound destinations doesn't care how cleverly the request was phrased — it moves from 'can we recognize this is an attack' to 'can this succeed even if we can't recognize it'
Because prompt-based detection is technically impossible to implement at all
Because egress filtering also improves the model's reasoning accuracy
explanation: This is the more robust posture whenever operationally feasible: a deterministic boundary succeeds regardless of how sophisticated the crafted prompt is, unlike a probabilistic classifier.

promptText: A dedicated prompt-injection filter service sits upstream of an agent and reports a "pass" verdict. Should this be sufficient to skip the deterministic tool-execution-layer authorization checks?
options: Yes, since a dedicated classifier is by definition more reliable than a generic downstream check

No — an upstream classifier has a nonzero false-negative rate by construction, and its failure mode is correlated with exactly the sophisticated, novel payloads most likely to be dangerous; the classifier should be an additive, cheap early-rejection layer, never a substitute for deterministic authorization
Yes, but only for tools marked readOnlyHint
No, because upstream classifiers are always slower than downstream authorization checks
explanation: Treating an upstream classifier's pass as license to relax the deterministic layer is one of the most common and dangerous architectural mistakes — an attacker capable of fooling the classifier is also capable of crafting something genuinely harmful.

promptText: A single mitigation (an injection classifier) independently catches 80% of attacks (a 20% miss rate). If three such independently-failing layers are stacked, what is the approximate probability an attack slips through all three, and what critical caveat governs this math?
options: Roughly 0.8% (0.2 x 0.2 x 0.2), but only if the layers actually fail independently — if all three share the same underlying failure mechanism (e.g., all are LLM-based classifiers), they are correlated and the multiplication does not hold
Roughly 60%, and this always holds regardless of how the layers are implemented
Exactly 20%, since adding more layers of the same type never changes the combined miss rate
Roughly 0.08%, and correlation between layers only strengthens this result further
explanation: This is the mathematical justification for defense-in-depth, but the multiplication of miss rates only holds when layers fail independently — genuine defense-in-depth requires at least one non-model-based, deterministic layer.

promptText: An agent has full customer-record access but should only ever answer shipping-status questions. What is the most robust way to prevent disclosure of unrelated PII (payment details, etc.) even under adversarial prompting?
options: Add a stronger instruction to the system prompt telling the model to only discuss shipping information

Enforce it at the data layer: the tool that fetches the customer record should itself only return shipping-relevant fields (tracking number, status, estimated delivery), so unrelated PII is structurally absent from the context and cannot be disclosed no matter how the model is manipulated — data that was never retrieved can't be leaked
Rely on the model's built-in safety training to refuse requests for unrelated PII
Encrypt the full customer record before placing it in the prompt so the model cannot read it but can still cite it
explanation: Field-level response filtering at the tool boundary is a deterministic control; instructing the model to self-restrict is a probabilistic one that a sufficiently adversarial prompt can override — this is exactly the case where the deterministic version should do the actual work.
